steps.instruction: Read Regular -er verbs; explain the French grammar in your own words.
Recall the words and build the lesson sentences, then check and retry.

Role-play Étudier ensemble with a patient classmate. Use regular -er verbs: say J'étudie, tu étudies, nous étudions. Ask Tu étudies avec moi aujourd'hui ? grammarNotes.explanation: French -er verbs are regular in most forms. Remove -er to get the stem, then add: je -e, tu -es, il/elle -e, nous -ons, ils/elles -ent. The -ent ending is silent in speech, so ils parlent and il parle sound the same. Étudier follows the same pattern: j'étudie, tu étudies, nous étudions, ils étudient. Note the elision before a vowel: j'étudie, not je étudie.
grammarNotes.caution: Not every -er verb is regular. Aller (je vais) is irregular, and manger changes spelling to mangeons. Lesson 1 uses only regular verbs.

grammarNotes.explanation: Manger is regular but needs an extra e before -ons to keep the soft g sound: nous mangeons. The other forms follow the -er pattern: je mange, tu manges, il mange, ils mangent. Boire, lire and comprendre are NOT regular: boire is je bois, nous buvons; lire is je lis, nous lisons; comprendre is je comprends, nous comprenons, ils comprennent. Learn these as separate patterns.
irregularNotes: boire: je bois, tu bois, il boit, nous buvons, ils boivent
lire: je lis, tu lis, il lit, nous lisons, ils lisent
comprendre (like prendre): je comprends, tu comprends, il comprend, nous comprenons, ils comprennent

grammarNotes.explanation: Regular -ir verbs of the finir type insert -iss- in the plural: nous finissons, ils finissent. Singular forms are je finis, tu finis, il finit. Do NOT apply this pattern to the verbs in this lesson's sentences: vivre (je vis, nous vivons) and écrire (j'écris, nous écrivons) are -re verbs; ouvrir (j'ouvre, nous ouvrons) takes -er-type endings but is irregular; recevoir (je reçois, nous recevons) is irregular. Mark these as exceptions when you learn them.
irregularNotes: vivre: je vis, tu vis, il vit, nous vivons, ils vivent
écrire: j'écris, tu écris, il écrit, nous écrivons, ils écrivent
ouvrir: j'ouvre, tu ouvres, il ouvre, nous ouvrons, ils ouvrent
recevoir: je reçois, tu reçois, il reçoit, nous recevons, ils reçoivent

grammarNotes.explanation: In French, an adjective generally agrees with the noun it describes in gender and number. For many adjectives, add -e for feminine and -s for plural: petit, petite, petits, petites. Rouge already ends in -e, so masculine and feminine singular look alike; the plural is rouges. French adjectives often follow the noun (un sac rouge), though common adjectives such as petit usually precede it (un petit cahier). Spoken final -s is normally silent.
grammarNotes.caution: The article also changes with the noun: un sac, une trousse, des sacs. Not every adjective forms its feminine simply by adding -e.

grammarNotes.explanation: A French possessive determiner agrees with the thing possessed. Say mon cahier but ma table, and mes livres in the plural. The owner may be male or female: son téléphone can mean his phone or her phone; context tells you whose it is. Before a feminine noun beginning with a vowel or mute h, use mon, ton or son for pronunciation: mon amie.

model.first_singular: mon cahier / ma table / mes livres
model.second_singular: ton cahier / ta table / tes crayons
model.third_singular: son téléphone / sa table / ses livres

grammarNotes.caution: Son does not by itself reveal whether the owner is a man or a woman. A person's name or sentence context resolves that ambiguity.

grammarNotes.explanation: Avoir is irregular: j'ai, tu as, il/elle a, nous avons, vous avez, ils/elles ont. French uses avoir where English uses be for hunger and thirst: j'ai faim (I am hungry), elle a soif (she is thirsty). For possession, use j'ai un livre or nous avons de l'eau. Je shortens to j' before ai.
grammarNotes.caution: Do not translate 'I am hungry' as je suis faim. Say j'ai faim. Avoir can also appear in other fixed expressions learned later.
